question.text: Which of the following gives the value of the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} yx^23^{x+y} \ \textrm{d}A$ over the rectangle $R= [1,3] \times [0,2]?$
question.explanation:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals, as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} yx^23^{x+y} \, \textrm{d}A &= \iint\limits_{R} y\, x^2\,3^{x} \, 3^{y} \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_{R} (x^2\, 3^{x}) \ (y\,3^{y}) \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \Bigg( \int_1^{3} x^2\,3^{x} \, \textrm{d}x \Bigg) \Bigg( \int_0^2 y\,3^{y} \, \textrm{d}y \Bigg) \end{align*}

question.text: Which of the following gives the value of the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} x^2y^3\ e^{2x-y} \: \textrm{d}A$ over the rectangle $R= [0,1] \times [2,5]?$
question.explanation:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals, as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} x^2y^3\ e^{2x-y} \: \textrm{d}A &= \iint\limits_{R} \big( x^2\, e^{2x} \big) \bigg( \dfrac{y^{3}}{e^y} \bigg) \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \Bigg( \int_0^{1} x^2 \, e^{2x} \, \textrm{d}x \Bigg) \Bigg( \int_2^5 \dfrac{y^{3}}{e^y} \, \textrm{d}y \Bigg) \end{align*}

question.text: Which of the following gives the value of the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} \sqrt{xy}\ \dfrac{1}{y} \: \textrm{d}A$ over the rectangle $R= [0,5] \times [3,7]?$
question.explanation:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals, as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} \sqrt{xy}\ \dfrac{1}{y} \: \textrm{d}A &= \iint\limits_{R} x^{1/2} \, y^{1/2} \, y^{-1}\: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_{R} (x^{1/2}) \ (y^{-1/2}) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \Bigg( \int_0^{5} \sqrt{x} \, \textrm{d}x \Bigg) \Bigg( \int_3^7 \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y}} \, \textrm{d}y \Bigg) \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} \sin{x} \ e^{y} \, \textrm{d}A$ over the rectangle $R= [0,\pi] \times [0,1].$
question.explanation:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} \sin{x} \ e^{y} \, \textrm{d}A &= \iint\limits_{R} (\sin{x}) \ (e^{y}) \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \Bigg( \int_0^{\pi} \sin{x} \, \textrm{d}x \Bigg) \Bigg( \int_0^1 e^{y} \, \textrm{d}y \Bigg) \\[5pt] &= \Big[-\cos{x}\Big]_0^{\pi} \cdot \Big[ e^y \Big]_0^1 \\[5pt] &= -(\cos{\pi} - \cos{0}) \cdot (e^1-e^0) \\[5pt] &= -(-1-1) \cdot (e-1) \\[5pt] &= 2(e-1) \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} \dfrac{y^2+1}{x} \, \textrm{d}A$ over the rectangle $R= [1,e] \times [0,3].$
question.explanation:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} \dfrac{y^2+1}{x} \, \textrm{d}A &= \iint\limits_{R} \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)(y^2+1) \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \Bigg( \int_1^{e} \dfrac{1}{x} \, \textrm{d}x \Bigg) \Bigg( \int_0^3 (y^2+1) \, \textrm{d}y \Bigg) \\[5pt] &= \Big[\ln {x} \Big]_1^{e} \cdot \Big[ \dfrac{y^3}{3} + y \Big]_0^3 \\[5pt] &= (\ln e - \ln{1}) \cdot \left(\dfrac{3^3}{3} + 3 \right) \\[5pt] &= 1 \cdot 12 \\[5pt] &= 12 \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} \dfrac{1+x\sin{y}}{x} \, \textrm{d}A$, where $R= [1,e] \times [0,\pi].$
question.explanation:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} \dfrac{1+x\sin{y}}{x} \, \textrm{d}A &= \iint\limits_{R} \left( \dfrac{1}{x}+\sin{y} \right) \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_{R} \dfrac{1}{x}\ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{R} \sin{y} \ \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} \dfrac{1}{x} \ \textrm{d}A %&= (d-c) \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm{d}x \\ &= (\pi-0)\int_{1}^{e} \dfrac{1}{x} \, \textrm{d}x \\ &= \pi \cdot \big[\ln|x|\big]_{1}^{e} \\[5pt] &= \pi( \ln {e}- \ln{1}) \\[5pt] &= \pi. \end{align*}

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} \sin{y} \ \textrm{d}A %&= (b-a) \int_c^d g(y) \, \textrm{d}y \\ &= (e-1)\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin{y} \, \textrm{d}y \\ &= (e-1)\big[-\cos{y}\big]_{0}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= (e-1)(-\cos{\pi} + \cos{0}) \\[5pt] &= 2(e-1). \end{align*}

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} \dfrac{1+x\sin{y}}{x} \, \textrm{d}A = \pi + 2(e-1) = 2e + \pi -2. \end{align*}

question.text: Calculate $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} (1 - 3x^2 + 2y) \: \textrm{d}A$, where $R= [-1,1] \times [0,1].$
question.explanation:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} (1 - 3x^2 + 2y) \: \textrm{d}A &= \iint\limits_{R} \textrm{d}A - \iint\limits_{R} 3x^2 \ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{R} 2y \ \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

The first integral is the double integral of unity:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} \textrm{d}A = \text{Area}(R) =2\cdot 1 = 2 \end{align*}

The function under the second integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} 3x^2 \ \textrm{d}A %&= (d-c) \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm{d}x &= (1-0)\int_{-1}^{1} 3x^2 \, \textrm{d}x \\ &= \big[x^3\big]_{-1}^{1} \\[5pt] &= 1^3 - (-1)^3 \\[5pt] &= 2. \end{align*}

The function under the third integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} 2y \ \textrm{d}A %&= (b-a) \int_c^d g(y) \, \textrm{d}y \\ &= (1-(-1))\int_{0}^{1} 2y \, \textrm{d}y \\ &= 2\big[y^2\big]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= 2(1^2 - 0^2) \\[5pt] &= 2. \end{align*}

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} (1 - 3x^2 + 2y) \: \textrm{d}A = 2 - 2 + 2 = 2. \end{align*}

question.text: Calculate $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} \left(4y^3 - 2x\right) \textrm{d}A$, where $R= [2,5] \times [0,3].$
question.explanation:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} \left(4y^3 - 2x\right) \textrm{d}A &= \iint\limits_{R}4y^3 \ \textrm{d}A - \iint\limits_{R} 2x \ \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

The function under the first integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} 4y^3 \ \textrm{d}A %&= (d-c) \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm{d}x &= (5-2)\int_{0}^{3} 4y^3 \, \textrm{d}y \\ &= 3 \big[y^4\big]_{0}^{3} \\[5pt] &= 3\left(3^4 - 0^4\right) \\[5pt] &= 243. \end{align*}

The function under the second integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} 2x \ \textrm{d}A %&= (b-a) \int_c^d g(y) \, \textrm{d}y \\ &= (3-0)\int_{2}^{5} 2x \, \textrm{d}y \\ &= 3\big[x^2\big]_{2}^{5} \\[5pt] &= 3\left(5^2 - 2^2\right) \\[5pt] &= 63. \end{align*}

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} \left(4y^3 - 2x\right) \: \textrm{d}A = 243 -63 = 180. \end{align*}

question.text: Calculate $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} \left(5x^4 + 9y^2\right) \textrm{d}A$, where $R= [-1,1] \times [0,1].$
question.explanation:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} \left(5x^4 + 9y^2\right) \textrm{d}A &= \iint\limits_{R}5x^4\ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{R} 9y^2 \ \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} 5x^4 \ \textrm{d}A %&= (d-c) \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm{d}x &= (1-0)\int_{-1}^{1} 5x^4 \, \textrm{d}x \\ &= \left( x^5\Big|_{-1}^{1} \right) \\[5pt] &= 1 ^5 - (-1)^5\\[5pt] &= 2. \end{align*}

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} 9y^2 \ \textrm{d}A %&= (b-a) \int_c^d g(y) \, \textrm{d}y \\ &= (1-(-1))\int_{0}^{1} 9y^2 \, \textrm{d}y \\ &= 2\cdot \left( 3y^3 \Big|_{0}^{1} \right) \\[5pt] &= 6\left(1^3 -0^3\right) \\[5pt] &= 6. \end{align*}

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} \left(5x^4 + 9y^2\right) \: \textrm{d}A = 2 + 6 = 8. \end{align*}

question.text: Calculate $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} (2-2x+ 9y^2) \: \textrm{d}A$, where $R= [0,2] \times [-1,2].$
question.explanation:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} (2-2x+ 9y^2) \: \textrm{d}A &= \iint\limits_{R} 2\,\textrm{d}A - \iint\limits_{R}2x \ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{R} 9y^2 \ \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

The first integral is the double integral of a constant, so we have:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} 2\,\textrm{d}A &= 2\iint\limits_{R} \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= 2\text{Area}(R) \\[5pt] &=2\cdot (2-0)\cdot (2-(-1)) \\[5pt] &=2\cdot 2\cdot 3 \\[5pt] &= 12 \end{align*}

The function under the second integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} 2x \ \textrm{d}A %&= (d-c) \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm{d}x &= (2-(-1))\int_{0}^{2} 2x \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 3 \big[x^2\big]_{0}^{2} \\[5pt] &= 3\left(2^2- 0^2\right) \\[5pt] &= 12. \end{align*}

The function under the third integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} 9y^2 \ \textrm{d}A %&= (b-a) \int_c^d g(y) \, \textrm{d}y \\ &= (2-0)\int_{-1}^{2} 9y^2 \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\big[3y^3\big]_{-1}^{2} \\[5pt] &=6\left(2^3- (-1)^3\right) \\[5pt] &= 54. \end{align*}

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} (2-2x+ 9y^2) \: \textrm{d}A =12 - 12 + 54 = 54. \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $C$ and $D$ are finite, non-overlapping regions and that \[ \iint\limits_{C} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = \dfrac12, \qquad \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = \dfrac32, \] find the value of \[ \iint\limits_{C \cup D} \dfrac{ f(x,y)}2\ \textrm{d}A. \]
question.explanation:
Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{C \cup D} \dfrac{ f(x,y)}2 \ \textrm{d}A &= \dfrac12 \iint\limits_{C \cup D} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \dfrac12 \Bigg( \iint\limits_{C} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A \Bigg) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac12 \left( \dfrac12+ \dfrac32 \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac12\cdot 2\\[5pt] &= 1 \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{C \cup D} -2f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A &= -2\cdot\!\!\! \iint\limits_{C \cup D} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &=-2\cdot \Bigg( \iint\limits_{C} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A \Bigg) \\[5pt] &= -2\cdot \left( -3 + 5 \right) \\[5pt] &= -4 \end{align*}

Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{C \cup D} 5f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A &= 5 \iint\limits_{C \cup D} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= 5 \Bigg( \iint\limits_{C} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A \Bigg) \\[5pt] &= 5 \left( 7 + 1 \right) \\[5pt] &= 40 \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A$, where \[ f(x,y) = \begin{cases} 6x, \quad & \textrm{if} \quad 0 \lt x \lt 1, \quad -1 \lt y \lt 0, \\[3pt] e^{x+y}, \quad &\textrm{if} \quad 0 \lt x \lt 1, \quad 0 \lt y \lt 1, \end{cases} \] and $R$ is the domain of $f.$
question.explanation:
First, notice that we have $R = R_1 \cup R_2$, where $R_1= (0,1) \times (-1,0) $ and $R_2= (0,1) \times (0,1).$ So, we can write

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A = &= \iint\limits_{R_1} f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{R_2} f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_{R_1} 6x \, \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{R_2} e^{x+y} \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_{R_1} 6x \, \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{R_2} \big(e^{x}\big) \big(e^{y}\big) \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= (0-(-1)) \int\limits_{0}^{1} 6x \, \textrm{d}x + \Bigg( \int\limits_{0}^{1} e^{x} \, \textrm{d}x \Bigg) \Bigg( \int\limits_{0}^{1} e^{y} \, \textrm{d}y \Bigg) \\[5pt] &= \big[ 3x^2 \big]_{0}^{1} + \big[ e^x \big]_{0}^{1} \cdot \big[ e^y \big]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= 3 + (e-1)^2 \\[5pt] &= e^2-2e+4. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A$, where \[ f(x,y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{2}x, \quad & \textrm{if} \quad -2 \lt x \lt 0, \quad 1 \lt y \lt 3, \\[3pt] \dfrac{x}{y}, \quad &\textrm{if} \quad 0 \lt x \lt 2, \quad 1 \lt y \lt 3, \end{cases} \] and $R$ is the domain of $f.$
question.explanation: First, notice that we have $R = R_1 \cup R_2$, where $R_1= (-2,0) \times (1,3) $ and $R_2= (0,2) \times (1,3).$ So, we can write \begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A &= \iint\limits_{R_1} f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{R_2} f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_{R_1} \dfrac{1}{2}x \, \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{R_2} \dfrac{x}{y} \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \iint\limits_{R_1} x \, \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{R_2} \big(x\big) \bigg(\dfrac{1}{y}\bigg) \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}(3-1) \int\limits_{-2}^{0} x \, \textrm{d}y + \Bigg( \int\limits_{0}^{2} x \, \textrm{d}x \Bigg) \Bigg( \int\limits_{1}^{3} \dfrac{1}{y} \, \textrm{d}y \Bigg) \\[5pt] &= \bigg[ \dfrac{x^2}{2} \bigg]_{-2}^{0} + \bigg[ \dfrac{x^2}{2} \bigg]_{0}^{2} \cdot \bigg[ \ln|y| \bigg]_{1}^{3} \\[5pt] &= (0 - 2) + (2-0) \cdot \big( \ln(3) - \ln(1) \big) \\[5pt] &= - 2 + 2\big( \ln(3) - 0 \big) \\[5pt] &= 2\ln(3)-2. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A$, where \[ f(x,y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{3x^2}{y}, \quad & \textrm{if} \quad -1 \lt x \lt 2, \quad 1 \lt y \lt e, \\[3pt] xy, \quad &\textrm{if} \quad 2 \lt x \lt 4, \quad 1 \lt y \lt e, \end{cases} \] and $R$ is the domain of $f.$
question.explanation:
First, notice that we have $R = R_1 \cup R_2$, where $R_1= (-1,2) \times (1,e) $ and $R_2= (2,4) \times (1,e).$ So, we can write

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A = &= \iint\limits_{R_1} f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{R_2} f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_{R_1} \dfrac{3x^2}{y} \, \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{R_2} xy \, \textrm{d}A\\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_{R_1} (3x^2)\left(\dfrac{1}{y}\right) \, \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{R_2} \big(x\big) \big(y\big) \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &=\Bigg( \int\limits_{-1}^{2} 3x^2 \, \textrm{d}x \Bigg) \Bigg( \int\limits_{1}^{e} \dfrac{1}{y} \, \textrm{d}y \Bigg) + \Bigg( \int\limits_{2}^{4} x \, \textrm{d}x \Bigg) \Bigg( \int\limits_{1}^{e} y \, \textrm{d}y \Bigg) \\[5pt] &= \big[ x^3 \big]_{-1}^{2}\cdot \big[ \ln{y}\big]_{1}^{e} + \left[ \dfrac{x^2}{2} \right]_{2}^{4} \cdot \left[ \dfrac{y^2}{2} \right]_{1}^{e} \\[5pt] &= (8+ 1)\cdot (1-0) + (8-2)\cdot \left(\dfrac{e^2}{2}- \dfrac{1}{2} \right)\\[5pt] &= 9 +3(e^2-1) \\[5pt] &= 3e^2 +6. \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Additivity Over a Rectangular Domain

question.text: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A$, where \[ f(x,y) = \begin{cases} 3y^2, \quad & \textrm{if} \quad 1 \lt x \lt 9, \quad -1 \lt y \lt 1, \\[3pt] \dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{xy}}, \quad &\textrm{if} \quad 1 \lt x \lt 9, \quad 1 \lt y \lt 4, \end{cases} \] and $R$ is the domain of $f.$
question.explanation:
First, notice that we have $R = R_1 \cup R_2$, where $R_1= (1,9) \times (-1,1) $ and $R_2= (1,9) \times (1,4).$ So, we can write

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{R} f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A = &= \iint\limits_{R_1} f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{R_2} f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_{R_1} 3y^2 \, \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{R_2} \dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{xy}} \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_{R_1} 3y^2 \, \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{R_2} \left(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}\right) \left(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\right) \, \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= (9-1) \int\limits_{-1}^{1} 3y^2 \, \textrm{d}y + \Bigg( \int\limits_{1}^{9} \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x} \, \textrm{d}x \Bigg) \Bigg( \int\limits_{1}^{4} \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt y} \, \textrm{d}y \Bigg) \\[5pt] &= 8\big[ y^3 \big]_{-1}^{1} + \Big[ \sqrt x \Big]_{1}^{9} \cdot \big[ \sqrt y \big]_{1}^{4} \\[5pt] &= 8(1^3-(-1)^3) + \left(3-1\right)\cdot (2-1) \\[5pt] &= 18. \end{align*}
